item.title: Loss, Grief, and Eventually Joy Once Again
item.description:
Grief

Loss, Grief, and Eventually Joy Once Again

Personal Perspective: Grief is a mix of disbelief, sadness, acceptance, and gratitude.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • In the beginning of our traumatic grief, we cannot fathom surviving such loss.
  • Our loss always remains and there are glimmers of joy.
  • Our memories of our loved ones provide internal support in our daily lives.

Over the course of my ten years of Psychology Today submissions, I have explored various topics within my own life’s journey. One of the most profound for me and my readers has been the experience of loss, grief, and surviving traumas to ultimately embrace joy with gratitude once again.

Marilyn and Barbara at Barbara's book signing (which Marilyn organized)
Source: bjaffe/blogger

After my best friend and sister-in-law Marilyn’s death, I examined such loss in my two Psychology Today posts: “Grief: From Darkness to Light (9/14/21), and “We Actually Can Survive Incredible Loss” (10/27/21). As I explored my personal heartache, I shared my daily ritual of saying "good morning" to Marilyn as my computer wakes to the screen saver. On display is the picture of us both taken during my book signing, which she organized for me (of course!). She beams with pride and amazement that her little sister wrote a book. “That’s my sister,” she would say when someone picked up the book to examine. “She’ll autograph it for you.”

With such a recent loss, I explored how it is even possible to live without her. I wanted the world to stop, rest on its axis, and suspend its movement. How did others laugh, eat, and play, when I was frozen in grief? But as the months have progressed, and I have slowly experience a lightness. I hear Marilyn’s quiet, steady voice within as I tell her about my day. “I’m always proud of you, Barbara. Keep going!”

Mar's first grandson, Max.
Source: bjaffe/blogger

After I wrote my post about Marilyn’s loss, a reader reached out to me. In her own tremendous grief, she found solace in my writing by substituting Marilyn’s name for the name of her lost love and, in doing so, she began to heal. She re-read my words daily and found herself slowly joining life again.

When Marilyn started hospice, she talked to me about her feelings, about dying, and about acceptance. While I wanted to deny her words, I listened. She also shared the joy of our friendship, stating, “We are so lucky. I don’t know anyone who has what we have had.” She embraced such gratitude, despite such sadness. Not once did she ever say, "Why me?" while the rest of us surely felt that way. And once again, she taught me the hardest lesson of all.

Marilyn and my brother Steve, who gave Barbara the best gift ever--Marilyn!
Source: bjaffe/blogger

Today’s writing purposely occurs on the 5th anniversary of Marilyn’s passing, for I needed to write; I had to write to honor Marilyn’s memory and to process my continued loss. I can instantly flash to those dreadfully painful weeks leading up to her death. Instead, I hold on to what I learned from her well-lived years. In my post, “My Friend Taught Me, and I Listened,” (2/28/22), I share one lesson I never wanted to learn from Marilyn but was forced to accept: how to die gracefully.

I write this entry today for myself. It is the way in which I make sense of the world, my world. When I feel pain, my tears transform into letters and words cathartically laced together. Yet, no words are enough to reflect my loss as well as my rich gains in loving and losing Marilyn. I honor her loss by living my life the way she would have wanted me to—fully! Grief is this way: a mixture of disbelief, sadness, elements of acceptance, all entwined with a deep love for the gifts from my dear sister and best friend.

Barbara's son Michael with his dear Aunt Mar, whom he adored.
Source: bjaffe/blogger

item.title: Transitional Objects and Memory
item.description:
Memory

Transitional Objects and Memory

How sports cards and other objects carry our memories.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • The term "transitional" refers roughly to the area between our internal world and the external world.
  • Transitional objects can offer comfort, love, memories, joy, consolation, tension-regulation, and play.
  • For children and adults, transitional objects might be a blanket, lovey, pet, ring, picture, or sports card.
Source: Mick Haupt / Pexels

Interestingly, it often turns out that issues in everyday life provide remarkable insights into psychology, psychoanalysis, and the internal working of the mind. I will start with the concept of transitional objects, and then discuss the meanings of these objects. Sports cards, especially baseball cards, are one of the most popular of "transitional objects."

In psychology and psychoanalysis, the term “transitional” refers roughly to the area between our internal world and the external world. In children, “transitional objects” might include a teddy bear, blanket, pet, lovey, and so on. In adults, these objects might be special items (a ring, a picture), books, a pet, and the like. These transitional objects can provide a variety of functions: comfort, love, memories, consolation, tension-regulation, joy, play, and more.

The psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott was especially helpful in showing us how transitional phenomena can help us reach our authentic, creative, less-defended parts. Winnicott suggested that it is creative self-awareness “more than anything else that makes the individual feel that life is worth living. Contrasted to this is a relationship to external reality which is one of compliance, the world and its details being recognized but only as something to be fitted in with or demanding adaptation.” (Playing and Reality, 1971, p. 65)

My colleague Tony Schaefer has run a world-class sports card collection business for over 30 years. He has a remarkable window on the world of transitional objects from childhood through adulthood. I asked him to share a bit about what transitional objects mean to collectors he's met. Here, Schaefer discusses these transitional objects from a psychological perspective, integrating the internal world, development, and everyday life:

"'It's just sports!' In one form or another, I hear that sentiment or read it on the internet often. It usually accompanies a story about fan overreaction or dollars spent on a new arena. However, I'm here to understand sports. In nearly 30 years as a sports card dealer, I've met so many great people through fandom, fantasy sports, and, of course, sports card collecting. Friendships and connecting with people are what life is all about!

As my card business grew, I noticed myself changing as well. I was less interested in the dollars and cents and more interested in the people I dealt with. I wondered about the "what" of their collections, as I found people were very creative in their quests. Then, I questioned about the "why." It turned out that these cards not only trigger nostalgia for their own childhoods but also generate a connection to history — to times before they were born and after they would die.

The history of sports intertwines with the history of civilization: Wars, civil rights, struggles, gender equality, labor issues, and so on. These cards are containers of memory. History, art, personal memories, and stories are kept very much alive in these little artifacts."

Tony asked a few collectors to express what their collections mean to them, not in terms of market value but what these objects hold and what holding onto them does for them. Their responses, below, further help to illustrate the concept of transitional objects.

“My collection, at its heart, reveals my philosophy that the only thing we have, ultimately as sentient beings, is memory. The present moment is a frontier that is infinitely small, before everything we feel, understand and remember is translated to memory, where it changes, settles and is sorted in some way that makes us who we are.

Therefore our memories are essential: they are everything, psychologically. This informs my belief that early childhood and adolescent memories are hugely important. I never trivialize them as an adult; I magnify them.

My collection isn’t just a way of cataloging memories that were meaningful to me, but trying to go back further generations into my father’s, grandfathers’ and great-grandparents’ memories. To capture stories of their childhood, stories that made our culture what it is.”

-John

“What would I hope my collection says about me? That I moved through the Hobby with an open heart. Connection runs through all of it – to my father and my son, to the friends this passionate pursuit has brought me, to those who have encouraged and helped me, and to the art, history, and stories kept very much alive in these little tangible artifacts.

And beyond connection, I’d hope it reflects something of who I aspire to be: a sense of justice, excellence, character and indomitability of spirit. I’d like it to show thoughtfulness and rigor, but also whimsy. It should reflect a seriousness about beauty, history, curation, and community – but joy and humor should always shine through.

That’s an awful lot of lifting for a dusty old pile of cardboard to do! If it does even a third of that, I’ll be lucky – but those are my hopes for when someday the collection is Final (though it will never be complete).”

-Nancy

“So you hear a lot of collectors say they collect sports cards because it gives them a link to the past – nostalgic reasons. Heck, I wanted a Cardinals Coca-Cola set because it reminded me of a time in my life – my early childhood – and a friend who I spent a lot time with growing up. It reminded me of grade school and a classmate who was (MLB player’s name redacted) daughter. Then that reminded me of watching my first World Series in 1982 and getting the 1982 Topps set as my big Christmas present that year. A true trip down memory lane. I can literally put myself back in the family room of my parent’s house in 1982 and remember the feeling of looking through those cards and pulling out the Cardinals and thinking about the World Series plays and highlights of Sutter, Porter, Ozzie, McGee, Herr, Hernandez, Oberkfell, etc. Wow! A feeling of comfort and nostalgia.

My collection as an adult is still about finding those items that bring me that same level of comfort and nostalgia. In some ways, like buying a seat in a time machine…I would chase cards that I had in my childhood. 1958 All Star Musial, 1959 Ken Boyer, 1964 Lou Brock, 1977 Topps Cloth Stickers, 1981 Ozzie Smith in a Padres uniform, and that 1982 Topps set, etc. I wasn’t really focused on value or long term investment but wanted to capture those good vibes from childhood.

Today, I value finding cards that have incredible history and provenance, and cards that give me the feeling of owning a true piece of history. All the rookie HOFers, all the Babe Ruth cards, all the Yankees and Cardinals greats. Holding a card that is 100 years old just makes me feel something…I can watch highlights of these players and feel something, but holding a physical object that has survived wars, survived the Great Depression, survived mothers who did vigorous spring cleanings, etc…is amazing to me. I think about the Civil Rights Movement when I hold Jackie (Robinson), (Satchel) Paige, (Willie) Mays, (Hank) Aaron, (Bob) Gibson, and even Curt Flood. I think about how the Babe was bigger than life and 'had a better year than the President!' I remember my grandmother retelling the story of the game where she saw Babe Ruth hit a home run in Sportsman’s Park!”

-Mike

As I mentioned above, transitional objects involve the connections between our internal and external world, our past and present. Tony Schaefer and John, Nancy, and Mike provide terrific examples of transitional objects and their importance to human beings. I am grateful to Tony and his colleagues for letting us enter their world.

item.title: How to Address Climate Change Denial
item.description:
Environment

How to Address Climate Change Denial

Many people deny climate change, but research shows how we can respond better.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • Heat waves and other extreme weather are worsening, but political immobilization and inaction persist.
  • We need to find ways to address the denial and minimization that prevent us from addressing climate change.
  • Recent psychological research suggests a path forward: targeted messages that draw on deniers' values.

As heat waves this summer shatter world records and dry up rivers and lakes, and wildfires pour smoke over thousands of miles, climate change is ever more apparent. Yet millions of people, including various political leaders, refuse to act. Vital questions emerge about why this is and what we can do about it.

Recent extreme weather is endangering countless species, including our own, but also provides a critical teachable moment. We should use these events to more fully develop and disseminate effective messages, drawing on commonly shared moral principles and narratives that have meaning to climate change deniers, and enhance education about addressing such political divisiveness.

Recent research indicates that altering attitudes about climate change is possible, yet such studies have not informed practice very much. We can make better use of this work.

How to Counter Climate Change Denial

Debunking misinformation with facts fails to alter public opinion, but targeted, strategic messages designed for particular audiences and reframing the issues in ways that appeal to these groups can help. Effective messages aimed at conservatives, for example, can appeal to values of national security, moral issues of purity, and religious beliefs about the need to steward the earth. Though climate change deniers frequently claim that they have a right to burn as much fossil fuel as they want, reframing might emphasize, for instance, the benefits of alternative energy sources that lead to energy and thus national security, the importance of family values that include the well-being of one’s descendants, and the purity and sanctity of nature as embodying divine creation.

Effective communication can also involve emotional appeals, instilling both sadness and guilt about the impact of climate change, and hope about possible solutions, and offering positive examples and moral arguments. People accrue short-term benefits from burning as much fossil fuel energy as they want, for instance, and have legal rights to do so, but these arguments are far outweighed by the longer-term harms (to current and future people and other species), the rights of countless present and future generations to lead healthy lives, and justice (since climate change disproportionately hurts poorer individuals and countries).

For evangelical Christians, the largest and most powerful voting block opposing efforts to reduce climate change, messages can highlight other narratives and values with which they are comfortable and familiar. This group is far less likely than others to think that climate change is occurring, or poses danger, or that the earth is warming primarily due to human behavior. Yet while these individuals are more likely than others to believe that God granted humans dominion over the earth (80 percent vs. 67 percent), even more (86 percent) also believe that God gave people duties to protect and care for the planet. The Bible, for example, tells us to serve as stewards over His creation and to recognize and respond to threats to ourselves and other species, which today we might refer to as climate change. In Genesis, for instance, Joseph correctly interpreted the Pharaoh’s dream and instructed him to store grain for an upcoming seven-year drought. When the famine occurred, only Egypt was prepared. Similarly, God commanded Noah to build an ark to save all species because 40 days of rain would arrive, causing a Great Flood—in other words, a climate catastrophe.

Yet these narratives about Joseph, and especially Noah’s Ark, are commonly viewed merely as Sunday School stories. We ignore the full implications. Noah, for example, protected countless species when cataclysmic flooding endangered them.

To alter attitudes and thus policy about climate, educators, religious leaders, policy makers, and the rest of us should use these approaches more. Many of us meet people who resist addressing the causes of our extreme weather, and we, too, can draw on this recent research to try to shift attitudes.

We should also enhance education for K-12, college, and the public about the need to think about moral conflicts using more systematic approaches, to know how to respond to flawed arguments by drawing on shared moral principles, and to invoke more than one of these values when needed.

The field of bioethics has, for example, developed a framework for doing so, invoking commonly endorsed values, including the need to examine all key relevant facts and consider major ethical principles: maximizing the benefits (to individuals and society), minimizing the risks, protecting stakeholders’ rights, and upholding justice (reducing inequities and avoiding undue burdens on vulnerable or disadvantaged groups). This framework can help, reminding us to take into account more than one principle (not just one that supports us most), recognize all facts (not just those that support our own view), and consider all stakeholders (including those who disagree with us and/or are most at risk of harms).

Though studies have started to probe how to shift public attitudes, more research is critically needed, and social scientists and others, including students, should be encouraged to pursue these topics more. Recent climate crises should lead not to suffering alone, but to creative brainstorming to develop novel ways of persuading others of the problem.

Otherwise, our extreme political divisions and weather will both only worsen.

A version of this post also appears on TheHill.com.
